title: Qdrant: Payload Filtering and Precision Tuning

questions.q: In Qdrant's filter language, which top-level operators correspond to SQL's AND, OR, and NOT respectively?
options: must / should / must_not
filter / exclude / require
match / range / nested
prefetch / rerank / fuse
questions.explain: The chapter maps must to AND, should to OR, and must_not to NOT, with conditions nested in a boolean structure like a SQL WHERE clause.

questions.q: What happens in Qdrant when you filter on a payload field that has no payload index?
options: The query fails with an error
Qdrant performs a full scan of all payload documents to evaluate the condition
The filter is silently ignored
Qdrant builds a temporary index automatically
questions.explain: Without a payload index, Qdrant evaluates filter conditions by scanning every payload document — effectively a sequential scan — so indexes must be created explicitly before those fields become efficient predicates.

questions.q: When does Qdrant abandon HNSW graph traversal and switch to brute-force search?
options: When the collection exceeds 10 million points
When quantization is enabled
When the expected number of filter-matching points falls below full_scan_threshold
When the query has no filter
questions.explain: If so few points match the filter that it is below the collection's full_scan_threshold, Qdrant switches to brute force over just the matching subset, which is faster than graph traversal for tiny result sets.

questions.q: Which quantization strategy gives roughly a 4x memory reduction, and what can recover most of the accuracy penalty for all three strategies?
options: Product quantization; larger ef
Scalar quantization; named vectors
Binary quantization; rescoring
Scalar (int8) quantization; rescoring
questions.explain: Scalar (int8) quantization cuts memory about 4x. Rescoring — re-ranking top candidates with full-precision originals — recovers most accuracy loss from scalar, product, or binary quantization.

questions.q: For multi-tenant SaaS, what pattern does the chapter recommend, and when should you abandon it?
options: Separate clusters per tenant; abandon it past 10 tenants
One collection per tenant; abandon it when queries get slow
A single collection with a tenant_id keyword-indexed payload field; switch the largest tenants to dedicated collections if one tenant's data is severely skewed
A collection per tenant; never use shared collections
questions.explain: The chapter recommends a single collection with a tenant_id payload field and keyword index for operational simplicity, switching severely skewed tenants (e.g., one holding 80% of the data) to dedicated collections.
